claims.text: Laser remelting of additively manufactured cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will refine its microstructure.
Laser remelting will improve the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi.
Laser remelting will reduce compositional segregation in AlCrFeNiSi.
Laser remelting will reduce residual stress in AlCrFeNiSi.
Laser remelting will reduce defect formation in AlCrFeNiSi.
Conventionally additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi has a coarse microstructure.
Conventionally additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi has elemental segregation, elevated residual stress, and relatively high defect density.
The proposed intervention is post-fabrication laser remelting with an optimized high-energy-density beam.
Rapid melting and resolidification will transform coarse dendrites or segregated regions into a more homogeneous, submicron-scale basket-weave structure.
Rapid localized laser heating and resolidification homogenize elemental distributions.
The laser melting-resolidification cycle relieves residual thermal stress.
Microstructural homogenization and residual-stress relief result in improved hardness and mechanical performance.
Laser-remelted AlCrFeNiSi will have 1.5- to 2-fold greater microhardness than the untreated comparator.
Laser-remelted AlCrFeNiSi will have lower XRD-measured residual stress than the untreated comparator.
Laser-remelted AlCrFeNiSi will have lower defect density than the untreated comparator.
Laser remelting refined an as-cast Al0.65CoCrFeNi alloy from coarse dendrites to a submicron basket-weave microstructure.
Laser remelting produced a 1.8-fold increase in Vickers microhardness in Al0.65CoCrFeNi.
The cited Co-containing, as-cast alloy result may transfer to additively manufactured cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi under comparable remelting conditions.
The comparison will use AlCrFeNiSi samples additively manufactured under identical conditions, with only one set receiving laser remelting.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, including less than a 1.5-fold hardness increase, no meaningful residual-stress reduction, or similar defect density, will falsify the hypothesis.
